input: In the case of the binary distillation that separates propane/propylene, the relative volatility is taken as 1.81, and this value is treated as though it remained constant over the column, which is a simplifying assumption that underpins the whole calculation. The specifications that have been set for the separation are quite demanding: the distillate is required to contain 98 mol% light component, whereas the bottoms is allowed to contain only 2 mol% light component, so a high degree of separation is being asked for at both ends of the column at the same time. When the well-known Fenske equation is applied under total reflux conditions, the minimum stage count that emerges from the calculation is 13.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler, and this figure is generally regarded as representing the absolute lower bound on the number of stages that any column performing this separation could possibly operate with. It is important to note, however, that the actual design does not operate at total reflux at all; instead, it works at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count that corresponds to that reflux is not obtained from the Fenske equation, but rather comes from a separate simulation that has been carried out for the design. Overall, the Fenske result should be understood as a benchmark figure, while the simulated stage count represents the design figure that is associated with the chosen operating reflux, and the two should not be confused with one another.
target:
Fenske minimum stages for the propane/propylene separation are determined from the product specifications at a relative volatility of 1.81, taken as constant over the column. The distillate specification is 98 mol% light component, and the bottoms specification is 2 mol% light component. At total reflux, the Fenske equation gives 13.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler as the minimum stage count.

Total reflux is the limiting operating condition behind the bound. At total reflux no product is withdrawn, the operating lines coincide with the diagonal, and each stage performs the largest separation the equilibrium relation allows, so no column separating the stated products can use fewer stages. The reboiler is counted in the total because the reboiler performs one equilibrium contact of the same kind as a tray. Constant relative volatility is the second assumption inside the result: the Fenske equation steps the composition ratio by the same factor at every stage, and a volatility that changed over the column would change the count obtained from the same specifications.

The actual design stands apart from the bound. Design reflux is a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation. Finite reflux needs more stages than the total-reflux minimum, and the simulation, not the Fenske equation, fixes how many more for this column. The bound also disciplines the simulation. A simulated stage count below the Fenske minimum would indicate an error in the simulation set-up or in the specifications it was given, because no simulation of the same separation can fall below the total-reflux bound.
